entry.title: Disruption with some GitHub services
entry.content:
Nov 19, 18:17 UTC
Resolved - Between November 5, 2026, at 18:02 UTC and November 19, 2026, at 18:05 UTC, GitHub users experienced unexpected expiration of their web browser sessions despite continued activity, requiring them to login. An authentication change introduced an issue that caused web requests to bypass the session activity updates and cookie renewal that normally extend session lifetime. Affected sessions consequently expired when they reached their initial expiration time.

We mitigated the incident by deploying a fix to ensure that continued web activity renews session expiration and browser cookies.

We are adding monitoring to detect unexpected drops in session renewal activity, helping us catch similar issues sooner and reduce their impact on users.

Update - The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

Monitoring - Starting around 18:02 UTC on November 5, GitHub web sessions stopped being renewed based on recent activity, so users were signed out when their sessions expired due to inactivity. These sign-outs were caused by a bug in session renewal, not due to a security incident.

We believe we fixed the bug at 05:23 UTC on November 19, and sessions created since then should renew as usual. We’re continuing to monitor the situation.

If you had an inactive session from that period, you may still find that you’re signed out when you return to GitHub. If that happens, all you need to do is sign back in.

entry.title: Incident with Pull Requests
entry.content:
Nov 16, 16:26 UTC
Resolved - On November 16, 2026, between 09:30 and 15:55 UTC, some pull request merges on GitHub timed out. On average, 2.9% of merge attempts timed out, with a peak of 7.1% at 15:17 UTC. Some GitHub Actions workflow runs triggered by pull requests were also delayed. Git operations such as push and fetch stayed available, with higher latency. This was a repeat of a shorter event on November 13, between 13:15 and 17:50 UTC, when 1.7% of merges timed out.

Both events had the same cause: some of the storage servers that hold Git repository data reached their disk read bandwidth limits. A merge must be written to every copy of a repository, so one overloaded server slowed merges for every repository it hosts. Read load on these servers had been growing as part of a planned move of repositories to new infrastructure. A disk configuration setting on those servers also made them read far more data than necessary, which cut their usable bandwidth roughly in half. We mitigated the incident by correcting that setting and moving some load away from the busiest servers.

The corrected setting is now applied permanently across our storage fleet. We are adding storage capacity in the affected region and alerting on per-server disk bandwidth so we catch saturation before it affects customers. Sustained merge timeouts will now page our on-call engineers directly. We are also adding capacity checks before moving repositories or traffic onto new infrastructure.

entry.title: Impact across multiple GitHub products including Actions, Pages, and Copilot products.
entry.content:
Nov 11, 21:21 UTC
Resolved - On November 11, 2026, from 20:05 to 21:02 UTC, customers experienced delayed or failed Actions workflow starts, webhook errors and delivery delays, slower GitHub Apps API requests, and reduced availability of Copilot features, including Code Review. GitHub Pages builds were also delayed.

Nearly all GitHub Actions runs triggered between 20:18 and 20:55 UTC were delayed or failed, leaving approximately 3.4 million partially created runs that are being canceled. No GitHub Pages deployments completed during the incident. In the Central US data residency stamp, between 20:06 and 20:50 UTC, about 63% of webhook API requests failed and 27% of deliveries were not recorded; those deliveries reached their destinations but remain unavailable to view or redeliver. Between approximately 20:20 and 21:00 UTC, Copilot code review on github.com completed 87% fewer reviews than normal and some other Copilot features were also unavailable.

The disruption was caused by an Azure Cosmos DB regional outage affecting database accounts used by these services. Per Cosmos’s RCA, a configuration change to the Central US gateways exposed a latent race condition under a specific high-load traffic pattern, causing gateway crashes and health-probe failures. Cosmos mitigated by rolling back the change. Service health recovered around 21:02 UTC, and the queued Actions backlog finished processing by 21:21 UTC.

Our follow-up work focuses on validating regional database failover across affected services and developing tested recovery procedures. We are also improving recovery tools to quickly clear stuck Actions checks and runs after incidents so they do not remain uncancelable or block pull request merges.

entry.title: Incident with Git Operations and Pull Requests
entry.content:
Nov 10, 17:55 UTC
Resolved - On November 10, 2026, from approximately 15:00 UTC to 17:55 UTC, GitHub experienced degraded performance affecting repository pages, pull requests, and GitHub Actions. Customers may have seen slow or failed page loads and delays processing pull request updates and merges. Some pull requests continued to display an earlier source-branch commit after the broader service degradation ended. GitHub Actions workflows were delayed for approximately 1.8% of events, peaking at about 7% between 16:30 and 16:50 UTC. Delays were typically 1.5 to 3.5 minutes, up to 10 minutes. Approximately 0.09% of pull request events did not start their workflows and needed to be re-triggered.

The degradation resulted from overload in the shared infrastructure that supports Git operations. Recent changes increased background processing and the work required to compute pull request merges, adding pressure to the same systems used by customer-facing requests. We mitigated the incident by disabling a recent merge-processing optimization, pausing background analysis, and temporarily limiting lower-priority traffic. The temporary limits also restricted access to commit pages for users who were not signed in. Background processing continued to catch up after service health recovered.

We have reduced repeated repository-analysis work and are adding workload-level concurrency controls to better protect customer-facing requests. We are also improving our procedures for safely reducing background load and making pull request synchronization more resilient to temporary failures.

entry.title: Incident with Actions and Checks API
entry.content:
Nov 9, 18:59 UTC
Resolved - On November 9, 2026, between 18:07 and 18:59 UTC, GitHub Actions experienced degraded performance. During this time, some customers saw workflow runs fail to start, update or report status correctly. An average of 28% of workflow runs were affected, peaking at 65% during the worst period of the incident. Once Actions services recovered, some jobs were left in a state that limited available concurrency until the runs were released.

The incident occurred during a planned migration of a core Actions database from GitHub’s datacenter to a new cloud region. After the migration completed, we shifted Actions service traffic to the new region. The volume of requests exceeded the capacity and rate limits configured there, so a portion of requests were rejected and workflow updates failed. Dependent services, including Webhooks, Pages and Copilot code review, saw secondary impact.

We mitigated impact by shifting some of the traffic back to the original region, allowing service traffic to remain within the configured limits. We then increased capacity and rate limits in the new region before gradually shifting traffic back. While this was a one-time migration event for this cluster that is now complete, we are improving how we validate capacity and limits before shifting traffic during remaining migrations, including shifting traffic in smaller steps. To address the stuck runs left after the incident, we are improving our ability to detect and mitigate these runs for future cases as well as readying an API to enable customers to address this themselves.

entry.content:

Until mitigation at 10:37 UTC, an average of 26% of webhook deliveries were delayed, peaking at 30%, and the backlog cleared by 11:40 UTC. Some deliveries were delayed by up to 3.5 hours, and delays for a small share began as early as 01:00 UTC. Actions skips events older than 30 minutes, so some workflow runs did not start.

The incident was caused by a degraded host that had slowed one of the cluster's Kafka brokers since November 7. The broker stopped reporting the metrics our alerts rely on, so we did not identify it until it stalled the cluster on November 9.

We mitigated the incident by removing the broker from service. We have since added an alert that pages us within 30 minutes when a host slows a broker this way, so we can remove the broker before it affects customers.

entry.title: Increased timeouts due to surge in anonymous users
entry.content:

Across that full window, 6.5% of recorded requests to github.com timed out, with a five-minute peak of 13.9% between 07:40 and 07:45 UTC. Release downloads were more affected: 38.5% of recorded requests timed out, peaking at 76% during that same five-minute interval. The two main error waves lasted about two hours and ten minutes in total, with recovery between them. The errors affected repository browsing and disrupted some CI workflows and Copilot code review jobs. Contrary to our earlier updates, follow-up analysis confirmed at least 6,236 authenticated requests that timed out, affecting activity feeds, access to uploaded attachments and repository archive downloads. Errors occurred during elevated traffic to our web infrastructure that handles unauthenticated requests. Impact was mitigated when traffic causing pressure on this system was alleviated. Our follow-up work focuses on improving capacity monitoring, traffic prioritization improvements, and automated protection against traffic spikes.

entry.title: Incident with Actions and Pages
entry.content:
Nov 4, 17:01 UTC
Resolved - On November 4, 2026, between 15:49 UTC and 16:48 UTC, and again between 17:20 UTC and 17:55 UTC, GitHub Actions, Pages, Webhooks, Code Scanning, and Copilot coding agent experienced delays. During this time, Actions workflow runs and job status updates were delayed by up to 25 minutes. Pages deployments dropped to about 4% of normal volume, webhook deliveries dropped to about 58% of normal volume, and Code Scanning analyses and Copilot coding agent sessions were delayed. Delayed events were processed after mitigation.

This incident was caused by a configuration change to an internal event-routing service that unexpectedly paused delivery of several event streams. The change depended on feature flags that were not set up as intended, which the service did not handle gracefully. We mitigated the first period by rolling back the configuration change at 16:14 UTC. The code change itself was not reverted by the rollback, so a subsequent deployment reintroduced it. We mitigated the second period at 17:40 UTC by rolling back again, then processed queued events and cleared backlogs.

We are taking several steps to prevent a repeat. The routing service will keep its existing behavior when a feature toggle is missing, so a misconfigured flag can no longer pause delivery. We are adding a pre-deploy check that each routing flag exists and is registered under the correct owning service, and we are making flag ownership less error-prone to set. We are also improving alerting so we detect paused event delivery sooner.

entry.title: Incident with Pull Requests, Git Operations and Issues
entry.content:
Nov 4, 11:50 UTC
Resolved - n November 4, 2026, between 09:35 UTC and 11:43 UTC, customers experienced intermittent errors and timeouts across GitHub.com, primarily on actions that write data. At peak, about 20% of pull request write operations (such as merging, commenting, and reviewing) failed, along with about 10% of issue creates and edits and 10–15% of project item edits. Git pushes over SSH, REST and GraphQL API requests, code scanning uploads, releases, and package operations were also affected, and about 1% of Actions runs were delayed by more than five minutes or failed to start. Overall, nearly 4% of all requests to GitHub.com failed at the worst point. Reads were largely unaffected, and retrying a failed action a short time later usually succeeded.

The incident was triggered by a burst of concurrent updates to the same database record, which tied up all available connections to one of our primary databases. Although that contention cleared, the backlog of waiting requests kept our database connection layer overloaded, and it did not recover on its own. We mitigated the incident by failing over to a new primary database host. Most services recovered by 11:31 UTC, and Actions recovered by 11:43 UTC.

Since the incident, we have disabled the code path that triggered the contention, increased the processing capacity of our database connection layer by 50%, and added alerting to detect this type of overload earlier. We are also improving our procedures so we can fail over sooner in similar situations.

entry.title: Increased task-related errors for Copilot Mission Control
entry.content:

Resolved - On November 4, 2026, between approximately 03:40 UTC and 10:01 UTC, some Copilot agent users experienced errors listing and creating agent tasks. On average, 1.22% of requests were failed, with a peak of 2.68% over a ten-minute interval.

The issue occurred when increased task-list traffic and expensive queries exhausted shared database capacity. We mitigated the broader impact by disabling a client experiment and temporarily restricting task-list requests from the affected client. Task-list requests remained restricted after the wider service recovered; we removed the blanket restriction on November 6 and continued a gradual rollout.

We’ve since improved task-list queries, moved rate limiting to separate infrastructure and added capacity monitoring. We’re continuing to reduce unnecessary client requests and validate capacity before expanding the rollout to reduce the chance of recurrence.

entry.title: Incident with Git Operations
entry.content:
Nov 3, 22:41 UTC
Resolved - On November 3, 2026, between 15:00 UTC and 22:37 UTC, Git operations over HTTPS on GitHub.com were degraded. Clones, fetches, and pushes over HTTPS were slow, and some failed. For about half of Git HTTPS traffic, median response time rose from under 100 milliseconds to as high as 5 seconds. On average, the error rate was 0.65% and peaked at 1.29% of requests to the service. Git operations over SSH were not affected.

This was due to a buildup of excess connections on the hosts that serve Git HTTPS traffic, which saturated their network capacity and caused slow and failed responses for all clients served by those hosts.

We mitigated the incident by blocking a client traffic pattern at our load balancers and reloading them, which released the excess connections. The block also prevented some users of one third-party integration from performing Git operations over HTTPS until we removed it on November 4 at 13:26 UTC.

We are working to alert on sustained Git HTTPS latency sooner and make load balancer mitigations take effect on existing connections immediately.

entry.title: Incident with API, Git, and Copilot requests
entry.content:
Nov 3, 13:56 UTC
Resolved - On November 3, 2026, between 12:34 and 13:51 UTC, some users experienced authentication failures and errors with the REST and GraphQL APIs, pull requests, Issues, and GitHub Copilot. On average, the error rate was 0.46% and peaked at 0.98% of API requests. Copilot API errors averaged 2.0% and peaked at 3.1%.

This was caused by a bug in our process for replacing control-plane servers in one of our compute clusters. When a replacement server did not receive a timely response from the existing cluster, it incorrectly created a separate cluster. This stopped traffic from reaching much of the cluster's capacity and overloaded the authentication servers that were still handling requests.

We mitigated the incident by removing the incorrectly configured server.
We are also fixing the replacement logic and adding safeguards to prevent servers in this state from serving traffic.
